Even now, through all her limbs, the gangrene of a bloody war creeps. It is no different in the whole world. Think on these things, Lipsius; and by this communion of miseries, lighten your own. And just as a slave used to be placed behind those celebrating a triumph, who in the midst of the joy of the procession would repeatedly cry out, **You are a man**: so let this monitor always stand by you, saying, **These things are human**. For as labor shared with many becomes lighter, so likewise does grief.

### CHAPTER XXVI

->*The Conclusion of the entire discourse. And a brief admonition to repeat and reflect upon it.*<-

I have deployed all my forces and my discourse, Lipsius: and you have what I thought should be said on behalf of Constancy against Grief. I hope these things are not only pleasing to you, but healing: and that they do not merely delight, but rather help! They will help, however, if you let them sink not only into your ears, but into your soul: and if you do not allow what you have heard to lie dormant and wither away, like seeds scattered on the top of the soil. Finally, if you will repeat and reflect upon them seriously. Because just as

<summary>Langius concludes his discourse by urging Lipsius to find comfort in the universality of human suffering and to internalize these Stoic lessons through constant reflection.</summary>
